docs.title: Workshop: Observability for Cloud Native
docs.text: This site contains the exercises to learn about observability.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Software developers and system administrators who want to learn observability.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: One day

docs.title: Expected knowledge
docs.text: Understanding of Kubernetes and container orchestration

docs.title: Goals
docs.text: Understand observability and its meaning in the context of cloud native infrastructure

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
40% theoretical introduction

60% practical exercises

The instructor will provide an introduction to each topic. Participants will then work on exercises. The instructor will be available to answer questions and provide hints. The instructor will also be able to demonstrate solutions to the exercises.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: All pages have the same navigation structure.

docs.title: Menu on the left
docs.text:
The left-hand menu contains the available chapters and displays the structure of the workshop.

On smaller screens or windows, the left-hand menu can be shown by clicking on the burger menu .

docs.title: Page contents on the right
docs.text:
The right-hand menu contains the contents of the current chapter and lists all exercises contained in the current chapter.

On smaller screens or windows, the right-hand menu can be shown by clicking on the burger menu and then clicking on the icon next to the current chapter.

docs.title: GitLab
docs.text:
This workshop is performed on a dedicated instance. It consists of an instance of Visual Studio Code for the web as well as a Kubernetes cluster.

You have been assigned a hostname and password for this instance, e.g.

seatN.inmylab.de;P4s5w0rd

This exercise will help you familiarize with the workshop environment.

You will not require the coding and version control features of Visual Studio Code for this workshop. It is meant as an interface for viewing workshop material and interacting with the Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: Task 1: Access your instance of Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
1. Go to https://seatN.inmylab.de where N is a number.
  2. Login using your password

Configure Visual Studio Code to your liking.

docs.title: Task 2: Access your Kubernetes cluster
docs.text:
The Kubernetes cluster is only accessible from within Visual Studio Code. The kubeconfig as been provisioned automatically.

  1. Open a terminal

  2. Examine the cluster:

    kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A

docs.title: You are ready!
docs.text: The workshop can now begin.

docs.title: LGTM Stack
docs.text:
In this exercise you will deploy the LGTM stack which consists of Loki, Grafana, Tempo and Mimir. It is also a an acronym widely used in software development meaning "Looks Good To Me". Afterwards, you will have the infrastructure to start collecting metrics, logs and traces.

This exercise assumes that you have access to the workshop environment with Visual Studio Code and the Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
You will deploy Helm charts for the components of the LGTM stack. Make sure your helm knows about the necessary repositories:

helm repo add grafana-community https://grafana-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

docs.title: Task 1: Deploy Mimir
docs.text:
Mimir is deployed as the replacement for Prometheus and offers long-term storage as well as a query engine built for high performance.

The values for the helm chart are available as file: container-slides/180_observability/020_lgtm/values-mimir.yaml. You can also view it in a web browser in the repository on Gitub.

helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    --create-namespace \
    mimir grafana/mimir-distributed \
        --values=values-mimir.yaml

Wait for the pods to become ready.

docs.title: Task 2: Deploy Loki
docs.text:
Loki is deployed for log aggregation and storage.

The values for the helm chart are available as file: container-slides/180_observability/020_lgtm/values-loki.yaml. You can also view it in a web browser in the repository on Gitub.

helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    --create-namespace \
    loki grafana-community/loki \
        --values=values-loki.yaml

Wait for the pods to become ready.

docs.title: Task 3: Deploy Tempo
docs.text:
Tempo is deployed for distributed tracing.

The values for the helm chart are available as file: container-slides/180_observability/020_lgtm/values-tempo.yaml. You can also view it in a web browser in the repository on Gitub.

helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    --create-namespace \
    tempo grafana-community/tempo \
        --values=values-tempo.yaml

Wait for the pods to become ready.

docs.title: Task 4: Deploy Grafana
docs.text:
Grafana is deployed for visualization and monitoring of metrics, logs, and traces.

The values for the helm chart are available as file: container-slides/180_observability/020_lgtm/values-grafana.yaml. You can also view it in a web browser in the repository on Gitub.

helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    --create-namespace \
    grafana grafana-community/grafana \
        --values=values-grafana.yaml

Wait for the pod to become ready.

docs.title: Task 5: Access Grafana Web UI
docs.text:
Create a port forwarding for Grafana:

kubectl --namespace=monitoring port-forward svc/grafana 3000:80

For Grafana to be accessible, Visual Studio Code must have port forwarding as well to provide access under https://3000.seatN.inmylab.de.

As soon as you have access to the Grafana web UI, you can login using the default credentials:

  • Username: admin
  • Password: admin

You will be forced to change the password on the first login.

docs.title: Task 6: Check datasources in Grafana
docs.text:
Check that the datasources for Mimir, Loki, and Tempo are correctly configured in Grafana. You can do this by navigating to the Grafana web UI, going to Configuration -> Data Sources, and verifying that each datasource is listed and has a green checkmark indicating it is working correctly.

Also, open all three datasources and click on the button labeled Test as the bottom.

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text: This exercise will start collecting data from the cluster.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
You will deploy more helm charts. Make sure your helm knows about the necessary repositories:

helm repo add metrics-server https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/metrics-server/
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

docs.title: Task 1: Metrics Server
docs.text:
The Kubernetes metrics-server plugs into the metrics API and collects resource usage data from the nodes and pods in the cluster. The data can be used from tools like kubectl top to monitor resource usage in real-time. In addition it enables the horizontal pod autoscaler to scale deployments based on resource usage.

helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server \
        --set=args[0]=--kubelet-insecure-tls

Check out the metrics collected by the metrics server using kubectl top pods in the different namespaces.

docs.title: Task 2: Tap existing data sources
docs.text:
When replacing Prometheus with modern components, you need to install the custom resource definitions (CRDs) for the Prometheus operator first. The are the defacto standard for declaring scrape targets metrics collection:

helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    --create-namespace \
    prometheus-operator-crds prometheus-community/prometheus-operator-crds

Grafana has consilidated the collection of metrics and logs from cluster components into a single uber-chart. This simplifies deployment but is rather complex to configure.

helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    --create-namespace \
    k8s-monitoring grafana/k8s-monitoring --values values-k8s-monitoring.yaml

The values for the helm chart are available as file: container-slides/180_observability/030_data/values-k8s-monitoring.yaml. You can also view it in a web browser in the repository on Gitub.

docs.title: Milestone
docs.text: Observability data will now flow from cluster components into the LGTM stack.

docs.title: Task 3: Check metrics
docs.text:
Go to the Explore view in Grafana, switch to the datasource Mimir and plot the following query to view the number of metric samples received by Mimir:

cortex_distributor_received_samples_total

The metric is a counter and should increase every few seconds.

docs.title: Task 4: Check logs
docs.text:
Go to the Explore view in Grafana, switch to the datasource Loki and plot the following query to view the number of lines received by Loki:

loki_distributor_lines_received_total

docs.title: Task 5: Deploy demo application
docs.text:
podinfo is a demo application that showcases various Kubernetes features such as deployments, services, and observability integrations: https://github.com/stefanprodan/podinfo.

You will deploy another helm chart for a demo application. Make sure your helm knows about the necessary repositories:

helm repo add podinfo https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo
helm repo update

Deploy the frontend of the demo application:

helm --namespace=default upgrade \
    --install \
    --set replicaCount=2 \
    --set backend=http://backend-podinfo:9898/echo \
    frontend podinfo/podinfo \
        --set=serviceMonitor.enabled=true \
        --set=extraEnvs[0].name=OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT \
        --set=extraEnvs[0].value=http://tempo.monitoring:4317 \
        --set=extraArgs[0]=--otel-service-name=podinfo-frontend

Test that the frontend is working correctly:

helm --namespace=default test \
    frontend

Deploy the backend of the demo application:

helm --namespace=default upgrade \
    --install \
    --set redis.enabled=true \
    backend podinfo/podinfo \
        --set=serviceMonitor.enabled=true \
        --set=extraEnvs[0].name=OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT \
        --set=extraEnvs[0].value=http://tempo.monitoring:4317 \
        --set=extraArgs[0]=--otel-service-name=podinfo-backend

docs.title: Task 6: Create a port forwarding
docs.text:
First, create a port forwarding using kubectl to interact with podinfo:

kubectl --namespace=default port-forward svc/frontend-podinfo 9898:9898

Then, create a port forwarding in Visual Studio Code for port 9898.

Now, open https://9898.seatN.inmylab.de.

docs.title: Task 5: Application-Level metrics
docs.text:
podinfo ships with a ServiceMonitor for exposing application-level metrics. Such a resource is automatically scraped by alloy.

Check out the ServiceMonitor for the frontend of the podinfo application:

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: frontend-podinfo
spec:
  endpoints:
  - interval: 15s
    path: /metrics
    port: http
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
    - default
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: frontend-podinfo

Check out the ServiceMonitor for the backend of the podinfo application:

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: backend-podinfo
spec:
  endpoints:
  - interval: 15s
    path: /metrics
    port: http
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
    - default
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: backend-podinfo

Check that data is being received for podinfo by running the following query:

scrape_samples_scraped{job="frontend-podinfo"}

docs.title: Task 6: Working with traces
docs.text:
podinfo is able to send traces to Grafana Tempo. You will need the port forwarding from above for this.

Execute the following command to query the frontend which will trigger a trace across both the frontend and the backend:

curl -svX POST -d foo http://localhost:9898/api/echo

The following query in TraceQL will filter for the traces you have just triggered:

{ .service.name="frontend-podinfo" } && { .service.name="backend-podinfo"}

You can also check that spans are received by Grafana Tempo by running the following query:

tempo_distributor_spans_received_total

docs.title: Visualization in Grafana
docs.text:
Goal

You will learn how to use Grafana:

  • Explore view
  • Create a new dashboard
  • Add panels for multiple signals
  • Configure visualization
    • Line/bar chart panels
    • Use left and right axis
    • Single stat panels

Resources

  • Use the official documentation of Grafana dashboards
  • Use the official documentation of Grafana panels and visualizations

docs.title: Preparation: Log in to Grafana
docs.text:
Create the port forwarding for port 3000 using kubectl and Visual Studio Code. See task 5 in the chapter about Grafana LGTM.

The panels you will create show the metrics of the demo application podinfo which you deployed in the chapter about data collection. Keep the port forwarding for port 9898 from task 6 in that chapter and generate some traffic so that the panels have data to display:

curl https://9898.seatN.inmylab.de/api/echo

Trigger a few errors as well - you will need them for the status code panels:

curl https://9898.seatN.inmylab.de/api/status/500

docs.title: Task 1: Create a new dashboard
docs.text:
1. In the main menu, go to Dashboards
  2. Click New and select New dashboard
  3. Click + Add visualization and select the data source Mimir
  4. Use the query up and click Run query
  5. Save the dashboard using the name Observability
  6. Set the auto-refresh interval to 10s using the dropdown in the top right corner. The panels you create below will then update on their own while you generate traffic.

docs.title: Task 2: Line chart panel
docs.text:
Add a panel to the dashboard which shows the request rate of the demo application as a line chart. The metric http_requests_total counts the HTTP requests of podinfo and is scraped from Mimir.

  1. Click + Add and select Visualization, then choose the data source Mimir
  2. Enter the query and click Run query
  3. Set the panel title to Request rate
  4. Set the unit to requests/sec in Standard options
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck)

Query:

sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="frontend-podinfo"}[5m]))

The default visualization type is Time series, which is a line chart.

docs.title: Task 3: Bar chart panel
docs.text:
Add a panel which shows the number of requests per status code as a bar chart.

  1. Click + Add and select Visualization, then choose the data source Mimir
  2. Enter the query and click Run query
  3. Switch the visualization type from Time series to Bar chart using the dropdown in the top right corner of the panel editor
  4. Set the panel title to Requests by status

Generate some more traffic, including errors using /api/status/500, and watch the bars change.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
sum by (status) (increase(http_requests_total{job="frontend-podinfo"}[5m]))

The status label of the metric contains the HTTP status code.

docs.title: Task 4: Multiple signals with left and right axis
docs.text:
Add a panel which combines two signals with different units: the request rate on the left axis and the 95th percentile of the request duration on the right axis. The metric http_request_duration_seconds_bucket is a histogram of the request durations.

  1. Click + Add and select Visualization, then choose the data source Mimir
  2. Enter the query for the request rate as query A and the query for the request duration as query B
  3. Expand the options of query B (below the query) and set Axis to Right
  4. Set the unit of the panel to requests/sec, then add a field override for the field of query B and set its unit to seconds (s)
  5. Set the panel title to Request rate vs. duration
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck)

Query A:

sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="frontend-podinfo"}[5m]))

Query B:

histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="frontend-podinfo"}[5m])))

Field overrides are configured in the tab All → Field → Overrides: Add an override for the field matching the name of query B and set its unit.

docs.title: Task 5: Single stat panel
docs.text:
Add a single stat panel which shows the total number of requests of the last hour.

  1. Click + Add and select Visualization, then choose the data source Mimir
  2. Enter the query and click Run query
  3. Switch the visualization type to Stat
  4. Set the panel title to Requests (last hour)
  5. In the Graph styles options, set Graph mode to Area so that the stat shows a sparkline of the values
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="frontend-podinfo"}[1h]))

docs.title: Bonus Task 1: Thresholds on a stat panel
docs.text:
Add another stat panel which shows the number of failed requests (status code 5xx) of the last hour and turns red as soon as any failure happened.

  1. Copy the stat panel from task 5 (panel menu → More → Duplicate) and adjust the query
  2. In Standard options, set the threshold: green at 0, red at 1
  3. Set the panel title to Failed requests
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="frontend-podinfo", status=~"5.."}[1h]))

docs.title: Bonus Task 2: Pie chart over the selected time range
docs.text:
Add a pie chart which shows the share of each status code over the currently selected dashboard time range - without editing the query when you change the time range.

  1. Click + Add and select Visualization, then choose the data source Mimir
  2. Enter the query and click Run query
  3. Switch the visualization type to Pie chart
  4. Set the panel title to Status code distribution
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
sum by (status) (increase(http_requests_total{job="frontend-podinfo"}[$__range]))

The variable $__range always contains the currently selected dashboard time range.

docs.title: Data Visualization for Logs
docs.text:
Goal

You will learn how to tap the data source for logs:

  • Discover which logs are available
  • Create simple queries
  • Filter logs
  • Filter structured data like JSON
  • Identify well-known errors like HTTP 404

Resources

  • Use the official documentation of Loki

docs.title: Introduction: LogQL
docs.text:
Logs are stored in Grafana Loki and queried using LogQL.

Every LogQL query starts with a stream selector. A stream is the set of log lines that share the same set of labels:

{service_name="kube-apiserver"}

The selector picks entire streams, not single lines. Everything after the selector is a pipeline which processes the lines step by step - for example line filters (|=), parsers (| json) and filter expressions:

{service_name="kube-apiserver"} | json | OriginStatus="401"

Finally, a pipeline can be wrapped in a range function to extract metrics from logs. This is what dashboard panels and alert rules use:

count_over_time({service_name="kube-apiserver"} |= "Unauthorized" [5m])

All pods in your cluster send their logs to Loki. The logs are collected by alloy and carry labels derived from their Kubernetes metadata. Your cluster provides the following sources:

Source Labels Content kube-apiserver, kubelet, etcd… service_name Kubernetes control plane logs frontend-podinfo, backend-podinfo namespace="default" Demo application LGTM stack and alloy namespace="monitoring" The observability stack itself

docs.title: Preparation: Log in to Grafana
docs.text: Create the port forwarding for port 3000 using kubectl and Visual Studio Code. See task 5 in the chapter about Grafana LGTM.

docs.title: Task 1: Display a first log
docs.text:
1. Go to Explore in Grafana
  2. Switch the data source to Loki
  3. Display all logs from traefik
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{app="traefik"}

docs.title: Task 2: Discover available logs
docs.text:
All pods in the cluster send their logs to Loki. The demo application podinfo runs in the namespace default. Display all logs from that namespace.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{namespace="default"}

Open the label browser to explore the available labels and their values. This is the easiest way to find out which sources exist.

Now narrow the result down to the backend of the demo application.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck)

Example:

{namespace="default", pod="backend-podinfo-0"}

(Replace the pod name with any one that is available in your environment. Use the label browser or kubectl --namespace=default get pods to find it.)

docs.title: Task 3: Filter using structured metadata
docs.text:
Filter the logs of the demo application and only display lines with detected_level="info". Loki assigns a level to every line during collection and stores it under detected_level.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{namespace="default"} | detected_level="info"

Depending on the Loki version, detected_level is stored as a label or as structured metadata. The query above works in both cases.

docs.title: Task 4: Filter JSON data
docs.text:
The demo application podinfo writes its logs as JSON. Restart the frontend of the demo application so that fresh logs are produced:

kubectl --namespace=default rollout restart deployment/frontend-podinfo

Filter for the log line in which the HTTP server of the demo application starts.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{namespace="default"} | json | msg="Starting HTTP Server."

Find out which version of podinfo is deployed. The corresponding log line contains the field version.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{namespace="default"} | json | msg="Starting podinfo"

Read the value of the version field from the expanded log line.

Now narrow the result down to the frontend of the demo application.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{namespace="default", pod=~"frontend-podinfo-.*"} | json | msg="Starting podinfo"

Optimize the query so that only required fields are parsed from JSON. This will make the query more efficient and easier to read:

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{namespace="default", pod=~"frontend-podinfo-.*"} | json msg, version | msg="Starting podinfo"

docs.title: Task 5: Analyze the logs of kube-apiserver
docs.text:
Display logs of kube-apiserver using the label service_name.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{service_name="kube-apiserver"}

Search the logs for unauthorized access (Unauthorized).

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 

{service_name="kube-apiserver"} |= "Unauthorized"
Let's hope the search returns no lines.

Filter for HTTP 401.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{service_name="kube-apiserver"} | json | OriginStatus="401"

docs.title: Data Visualization for Metrics
docs.text:
Goal

You will learn how to tap the data source for metrics:

  • Create simple queries
  • Work with labels and filters
  • Use funktions for analysis
  • Aggregate data

Resources

  • Use the official documentation of Prometheus

docs.title: Preparation: Log in to Grafana
docs.text: Create the port forwarding for port 3000 using kubectl and Visual Studio Code. See task 5 in the chapter about Grafana LGTM.

docs.title: Task 1: Display a first metric
docs.text:
1. Go to Explore in Grafana
  2. Switch to the datasource Mimir
  3. Make sure that Code is selected instead of Build (right hand side above the query)
  4. Use the query up
  5. Click Run query

The metric called up shows whether a target is available. It displays 1 for success and 0 for failure.

You will see many different instances of the metric up - one for each target.

docs.title: Task 2: Use labels
docs.text:
Check whether the targets for node-exporter are available. Create a query using the metric up and filter using the label job with the value node-exporter.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck)

Example:

up{job="node-exporter"}

Now filter for a specific instance of node-exporter.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck)

Example:

up{job="node-exporter", instance="10.0.0.1:9100"}

(Replace the IP address with any one that is available in your environment.)

docs.title: Task 3: Container CPU usage
docs.text:
The metric container_cpu_usage_seconds_total counts CPU seconds per container. It is a counter with the labels namespace, pod and container. Calculate the per second CPU usage (cores) with a 5 minutes sliding window. Exclude the pod level entries with container!="".

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!=""}[5m])

Sum the containers of each pod.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
sum by (namespace, pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!=""}[5m]))

docs.title: Task 4: Memory vs limit
docs.text:
The metric container_memory_working_set_bytes shows the memory that counts towards the OOM limit. Calculate the used memory per container in GiB.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""} / 1024 / 1024 / 1024

Calculate the percent of the memory limit used, with kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"}. Aggregate both sides to identical labels first, otherwise the label sets do not match.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
sum by (namespace, pod, container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""})
/
sum by (namespace, pod, container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"})

docs.title: Task 5: Restarts and top lists
docs.text:
Show which containers restarted in the last hour using kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
sum by (namespace, pod, container) (increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[1h])) > 0

Show the three containers with the highest memory usage.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
topk(3, container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""})

docs.title: Bonus Task 1: Peak memory
docs.text:
Calculate the peak memory per container over the last 24 hours, in GiB.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
max_over_time(container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""}[24h]) / 1024 / 1024 / 1024

docs.title: Bonus Task 2: Check for missing series
docs.text:
Write a query that returns a result only when no containers are running in the namespace shop.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
absent(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="shop", container!=""})

docs.title: Bonus Task 3: Combine metrics
docs.text:
Calculate the used memory in percent using the metrics node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes and node_memory_MemTotal_bytes.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes

The result is missing the hostname which is stored in the label nodename by the metric node_uname_info. Both share the label instance. Join the result from above with the second metric using the keywords on as well as group_left.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
(node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes) * on(instance) group_left(nodename) node_uname_info

docs.title: Data Visualization for Traces
docs.text:
Goal

You will learn how to tap the data source for traces:

  • Understand the structure of traces and spans
  • Create simple queries with TraceQL
  • Filter traces by attributes, duration and status
  • Follow a request across multiple services

Resources

  • Use the official documentation of TraceQL
  • The traces in this exercise are generated by the demo application podinfo which you deployed in the chapter about data collection

docs.title: Introduction: TraceQL
docs.text:
Traces are stored in Grafana Tempo and queried using TraceQL.

A trace represents a single request as it travels through the system. It consists of multiple spans - one per operation, for example an HTTP request to podinfo or the call to the backend. Spans carry attributes like the service name, the HTTP method and the duration.

A TraceQL query consists of one or more conditions wrapped in curly braces:

{ .service.name="podinfo-frontend" && duration > 10ms }

Conditions are matched against individual spans. Multiple expressions can be combined into spansets using && and ||. Structural operators like >> (descendant) and << (ancestor) relate spans to each other - this is what allows you to follow a request across services.

docs.title: Preparation: Generate traces
docs.text:
TraceQL only finds traces that were actually sent to Tempo. Create the port forwarding for podinfo and generate some traffic. See task 6 in the chapter about data collection.

Execute the following commands to trigger traces across both the frontend and the backend:

curl -sX POST -d foo http://localhost:9898/api/echo
curl -s http://localhost:9898/delay/1
curl -s http://localhost:9898/status/500

docs.title: Preparation: Log in to Grafana
docs.text: Create the port forwarding for port 3000 using kubectl and Visual Studio Code. See task 5 in the chapter about Grafana LGTM.

docs.title: Task 1: Display a first trace
docs.text:
1. Go to Explore in Grafana
  2. Switch the data source to Tempo
  3. Make sure that the query language is set to TraceQL (right hand side above the query)
  4. Display all traces from the frontend of the demo application
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{ .service.name="podinfo-frontend" }

docs.title: Task 2: Filter by duration
docs.text:
The command curl -s http://localhost:9898/delay/1 triggered a slow request. Filter for traces of the frontend which took more than one second.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{ .service.name="podinfo-frontend" && duration > 1s }

docs.title: Task 3: Filter for errors
docs.text:
The command curl -s http://localhost:9898/status/500 triggered a failing request. Filter for failed spans of the frontend.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{ .service.name="podinfo-frontend" && status = error }

docs.title: Task 4: Follow a request across services
docs.text:
Display only spans that belong to both services. This is the query from the chapter about data collection.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{ .service.name="podinfo-frontend" } && { .service.name="podinfo-backend" }

The result contains two spans: One for the frontend and one for the backend.

docs.title: Task 5: Use the structural operator
docs.text:
The query from task 4 finds traces containing both services but the two spansets are independent. The structural operator >> finds spans which are descendants of another span. This reflects the call hierarchy: The frontend called the backend.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{ .service.name="podinfo-frontend" } >> { .service.name="podinfo-backend" }

The result only contains the backend spans which are children of a frontend span. Using << instead would return the frontend spans which are ancestors of a backend span.

docs.title: Task 6: Filter by attributes
docs.text:
Display spans of the frontend for requests to the path /api/echo.

Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck) 
{ .service.name="podinfo-frontend" && .http.route="/api/echo" }

Depending on the instrumentation, the attribute is called .http.route or .url.path. Open a single trace and inspect the attributes of a span to find out which ones are available. Autocomplete in the query editor lists them, too.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Goal

In this project you will learn how to set up and test alerts in Grafana.

Afterwards you will get to know the Alertmanager and declarative alerting:

  • Install and configure the Alertmanager declaratively
  • Trigger test alerts and observe their delivery
  • Declare alerts as PrometheusRule and have them evaluated

Resources

  • Try to solve the tasks on your own. Each task has a collapsible block with a suggested solution in case you get stuck.

docs.title: Task 1: Create a receiver for alerts
docs.text:
Create a simple HTTP echo server deployment and service in the monitoring namespace. This will be used later as a webhook receiver for the Alertmanager.

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: httpbin-echo
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: httpbin-echo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: httpbin-echo
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: httpbin
        image: mccutchen/go-httpbin
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: httpbin-echo
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  selector:
    app: httpbin-echo
  ports:
  - port: 8080

XXX port-forwarding for svc/httpbin-echo:8080

kubectl --namespace=monitoring port-forward svc/httpbin-echo 8080:8080

XXX test

curl -s -XPOST http://localhost:8080/post \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data '{"message": "Hello, world!"}'

docs.title: Task 2: Install Alertmanager
docs.text:
Create a file alertmanager.yaml with the following content. Replace the smarthost with the value determined in Task 2.1:

config:
  enabled: true

  global: {}

  receivers:
  - name: webhook-echo
    webhook_configs:
    - url: http://httpbin-echo.monitoring:8080/post
      send_resolved: true

  route:
    group_wait: 10s
    group_interval: 5m
    receiver: webhook-echo
    repeat_interval: 3h
    routes:
    - matchers: ['severity="critical"']
      receiver: webhook-echo
      group_wait: 0s
      repeat_interval: 1h

  inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: ['severity="critical"']
    target_matchers: ['severity="warning"']
    equal: ['alertname']

Install the Alertmanager with this configuration:

helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm --namespace=monitoring upgrade \
    --install \
    alertmanager prometheus-community/alertmanager \
        --values values_alertmanager.yaml \
        --values alertmanager.yaml
Solution (Click on the arrow if you are stuck)

The route is deliberately kept simple here: All alerts go to the receiver shop-mail, which sends an email via Mailpit. Alerts with the label team="debug" go to the receiver webhook-echo instead. Check the installation with kubectl --namespace=monitoring get pods. The pod should be Running. You can check the applied configuration in the ConfigMap alertmanager under the key alertmanager.yaml.

docs.title: Task 3: Trigger a test alert
docs.text:
The Alertmanager accepts alerts via a REST API. First create a port-forward:

kubectl --namespace=monitoring port-forward svc/alertmanager 9093:9093

Trigger a test alert:

curl -s -XPOST http://localhost:9093/api/v2/alerts \
    --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data '[{
      "labels": {
        "alertname": "DiskAlmostFull",
        "team": "shop",
        "severity": "warning",
        "instance": "node-1"
      },
      "annotations": {
        "summary": "Disk usage above 90% on node-1"
      }
    }]'

Observe the alert:

  • Open the Alertmanager UI at http://localhost:9093 and take a look at the alert
  • XXX View alert in webhook

docs.title: Task 4: Declarative alerts with PrometheusRule
docs.text:
Alerts do not have to be maintained in a UI. They can be managed as a Kubernetes resource (PrometheusRule) to be evaluated automatically.

Create a file demo-alert.yaml with the following content:

---
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: demo-alerts
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: demo
    limit: 10
    rules:
    - alert: DemoAlert
      expr: vector(1)
      for: 1m
      keep_firing_for: 5m
      labels:
        team: shop
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: Demo alert for testing the alerting pipeline
        description: This alert is always active (value {{ $value }})

The expression vector(1) always returns a result greater than 0 - so the alert is guaranteed to fire. Apply the file:

kubectl apply -f demo-alert.yaml

XXX checkout the resource

kubectl delete -f demo-alert.yaml

docs.title: A second example: CPU usage relative to the limit
docs.text:
Real alerts are based on actual metrics. Create a file pod-cpu-alert.yaml with the following content:

---
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: pod-cpu-alerts
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: podinfo
    rules:
    - alert: PodHighCPUUsage
      expr: |
        100 * rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!="", container!="POD"}[5m])
          / on (namespace, pod, container)
          kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="cpu"}
        > 80
      for: 5m
      labels:
        team: shop
        severity: critical
      annotations:
        summary: Pod {{ $labels.pod }} uses {{ printf "%.0f" $value }}% of its CPU limit
        description: Container {{ $labels.container }} in namespace {{ $labels.namespace }} uses more than 80% of its CPU limit

The expression divides the CPU usage of each container by its CPU limit and compares the result to 80%. The matcher container!="" filters out metrics without a container, and container!="POD" filters out the aggregated pod metrics. The on (namespace, pod, container) clause joins the usage series with the matching limit series. Because the condition must hold for for: 5m, short spikes do not trigger the alert.

Note that the Alertmanager routes alerts with severity="critical" to the webhook-echo receiver with group_wait: 0s and repeat_interval: 1h - this alert therefore appears in the webhook sooner than the warning demo alert. Apply the file:

kubectl apply -f pod-cpu-alert.yaml

To see the alert fire, a pod has to actually approach its CPU limit. Check the value of the expression in Explore with the PromQL query above (without the > 80).

kubectl delete -f pod-cpu-alert.yaml
